questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z.$
questions.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{4}{{z}^{2}}\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{4}{{z}^{2}}\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[(-\frac{4}{z})]}_{2}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{4}{a}+\frac{4}{2}) \\  & =0+2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}\frac{5}{{x}^{2}}\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}5{x}^{-2}\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[(-5{x}^{-1})]}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{x}]}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-5\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =-5\cdot (0-\frac{1}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=1+{x}^{3}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=3{x}^{2}\,⟹\,\frac{1}{3}\text{d}u={x}^{2}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to \infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=1+{x}^{3}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{{(1+{x}^{3})}^{4}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{4}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-4}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{u}^{-3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{u}^{3}}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{a}^{3}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=2+{x}^{4}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}u=4{x}^{3}\text{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to \infty $ when $x\to -\infty ,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=2+{x}^{4}$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty $ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $2$ | $\infty $ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{(2+{x}^{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\infty }^{2}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to -\infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{(2+{x}^{4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{u}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Divergent Improper Integrals
questions.problem:
Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

- ${\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u$
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z$
- ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{1}{(u-1)^{3}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2(u-1)^{2}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}+\frac{1}{2(2-1)^{2}}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(a-1)^{2}}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{1}3{z}^{2}\,\text{d}z \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[{z}^{3}]}_{a}^{1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-{a}^{3}) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-2}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integral II is divergent.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-5}]}_{6}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2\sqrt{6-5}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{x}^{1/3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt[3]{a}-1) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals I and II are divergent.

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}\frac{1}{3x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{3}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x+1|]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3a+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3a+1|) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (\infty ) \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the integral is divergent.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{2}^{\infty }\frac{8}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}\frac{8}{{t}^{5}}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}{t}^{-5}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{4}{t}^{-4}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{{t}^{4}}]}_{2}^{a} \\  & =-2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }(\frac{1}{{a}^{4}}-\frac{1}{{2}^{4}}) \\  & =-2(0-\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Upper Limit Using Substitution
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we substitute $u=x+1.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u \to \infty$ when $x \to \infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x+1$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $1$ | $\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\int_0^\infty \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2} \,\textrm{d}x
=
\int_1^\infty \dfrac{1}{u^2} \,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{1}{(x+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\infty }{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to \infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }[\frac{1}{a}-\frac{1}{1}] \\  & =-1\cdot (0-1) \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating Improper Integrals With an Unbounded Lower Limit
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that, this time, it's the *lower* limit of integration that's unbounded.  

First, we substitute $u=x-4.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}= 1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}u =\textrm{d}x.
$$

Since $u\to -\infty$ when $x\to -\infty,$ the table for the limits of integration using the rule $u=x-4$ is as follows:

| $x$ | $0$ | $-\infty$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $u$ | $-4$ | $-\infty$ |

So, the integral in terms of the new variable $u$ is

$$
\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{0}    \dfrac{1}{(x-4)^2} \,\textrm{d}x
=\int_{-\infty}^{-4} \dfrac{1}{u^2}  \,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Finally, we proceed by setting the lower bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to-\infty.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}\frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{-4}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-4}{u}^{-2}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-{u}^{-1}]}_{a}^{-4} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[\frac{1}{u}]}_{a}^{-4} \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{(-4)}-\frac{1}{a}] \\  & =-1\cdot {lim}_{a\to -\infty }(-\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =-1\cdot (-\frac{1}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?

- $\displaystyle \int_1^\infty \frac{1}{\sqrt{x} }\,\textrm{d}x$

- $\displaystyle \int_{-\infty}^{-2} \frac{1}{(1+x)^2}\,\textrm{d}x$

- $\displaystyle \int_{1}^\infty \dfrac{1}{x^3} \,\textrm{d}x$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

- For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}{x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[2{x}^{1/2}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }{[\sqrt{x}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & =2{lim}_{b\to \infty }[\sqrt{b}-1] \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

- For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-2}\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-2}\frac{1}{(1+x)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{1+x}]}_{a}^{-2} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }[-\frac{1}{1-2}+\frac{1}{1+a}] \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }[\frac{1}{1+a}+1] \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent (not divergent).

- For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{b}{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{2{x}^{2}}]}_{1}^{b} \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }[-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2({1}^{2})}] \\  & ={lim}_{b\to \infty }[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{2{b}^{2}}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =\frac{1}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent (not divergent).

In conclusion, only integral I is divergent.
